title: Why learn a language if the app can do it?

turns.speaker: Jess
turns.text: My nephew's dropped German. He held up his phone and said the earpiece does it in real time now, so what exactly is he studying for.

turns.speaker: Mateo
turns.text: I mean, he's not wrong about the technology. It's genuinely good now.

turns.speaker: Freya
turns.text: It's good at transactions. Buying a train ticket, reading a menu, getting the gist of an email. Nobody's arguing with that.

turns.speaker: Freya
turns.text: Being liked. You can't be funny through a translation app. You can't be gently rude, you can't flirt, you can't say the thing that shows you understood the joke about the neighbour.

turns.speaker: Mateo
turns.text: That's true, although most people don't learn a language well enough to be funny in it anyway.

turns.speaker: Mateo
turns.text: What persuades me more is the delay. Even a second of lag kills a conversation. You end up taking turns at a device instead of talking.

turns.speaker: Jess
turns.text: And there's the trust thing. Would you sign something you'd only read through a translation?

turns.speaker: Freya
turns.text: There's also what it does to you rather than for you. Learning one properly rearranges how you hear your own language. That's not a service you can buy.

turns.speaker: Jess
turns.text: I'm not sure that'll persuade a fifteen-year-old.

turns.speaker: Freya
turns.text: No. Almost nothing does at fifteen.

points: Jess's nephew has dropped German because real-time translation earpieces exist.
Freya concedes the technology handles transactions well: tickets, menus, the gist of an email.
Her objection is social: humour, teasing, flirting and shared jokes do not survive translation.
Mateo counters that most learners never reach the level needed to be funny anyway, but is persuaded by latency, since even a second of lag turns a conversation into taking turns at a device.
Jess raises trust, asking whether anyone would sign a document read only through translation.
Freya's final argument is about the effect on the learner rather than the task: learning a language changes how you hear your own, which cannot be bought as a service.
